Downtown Business Owners: You Cannot Afford to Keep Paying for NDP's Mistakes

If you own a business downtown, you are required by law to pay a special assessment to the Nashville Downtown Partnership. Since 2004, those assessments have totaled roughly $60 million. The special assessment is not optional, and the business owners who pay it have never been shown the contract it funds.

This summer NDP sued Block for damages tied to the explosive June 2025 fire that devastated the Downtown Library Parking Garage. The lawsuit alleges the contractor stored combustible materials in the garage without a permit. Neither Metro Codes nor the Fire Marshal had ever issued a permit for fuel storage there.

The security contract is unusual. It is run through a recently created entity called NDMC PSO LLC, a shell company of the District Management Corporation, created by the same person who runs the District Management Corporation and who then hires his own firm, NDP, to manage the downtown security operations through it. That person is Tom Turner. The shell company has no employees of its own.

Tom Turner is the president of the Nashville Downtown Partnership. He also chairs the board of the District Management Corporation. The arrangement means Turner hires Turner, through a shell company that answers to Turner.

NDP's Director of Safety Services is David Corman, a former police commander who earned $116,943 in 2024 directing the private policing operation. Until recently, Corman's son served as Director of Administration at Solaren Risk Management, the firm staffing the off-duty troopers who did the actual private policing downtown. The private policing contract has never received Council approval for its expenditure.

This is private policing run through a shell company. A shell company with no budget, no employees, and no public accountability. The special assessment funds the private policing, but the business owners paying the special assessment cannot see what the private policing contract requires.

Christina Kane, a parking customer, said it is like nobody cares. David Corman, who leads the rival firm Solaren Risk Management, called the arrangement Operation Flood the Zone. The Metro Council will vote on the private policing contract next month.

The question is not whether downtown needs security. The question is whether a shell company, a special assessment no one can audit, and a private policing operation no one approved are the way to buy it. Council member Freddie O'Connell wrote on Twitter that the deal deserves real scrutiny.
